title: Build a Small API Consumer Using Structured Data
learningObjectives: Describe the purpose and scope of build a small api consumer using structured data.
Plan the required data, inputs, outputs, and behaviors.
Break the solution into manageable functions or steps.
Implement and test normal, invalid, and boundary cases.
Review the result and explain limitations and improvements.

understand.concept: An API consumer requests information from a service, checks the response outcome, parses structured data, validates the expected shape, and presents useful results. A robust consumer handles missing fields, empty data, timeouts, authentication errors, and rate limits. This project uses fictional or local test data and should avoid exposing credentials.
understand.whyItMatters: This project integrates communication, structured formats, parsing, validation, asynchronous behavior, and error handling.
understand.analogy: Think of completing a small real-world task by defining the goal, organizing the work, checking each step, and reviewing the finished result.
understand.analogyLimit: Software projects require precise requirements, data and code design, technical testing, and iterative change; the analogy only introduces a workflow.

explain.narrative:
An API consumer requests information from a service, checks the response outcome, parses structured data, validates the expected shape, and presents useful results. A robust consumer handles missing fields, empty data, timeouts, authentication errors, and rate limits. This project uses fictional or local test data and should avoid exposing credentials.

Build incrementally and keep the project scope appropriate for your current skills. The examples illustrate individual design steps; they are not a complete ready-made project. Test your own implementation and document assumptions.

examples.explanation: A structured response contains predictable fields.

examples.title: Handle empty data
examples.code:
const items=[];
console.log(items.length?'show list':'show empty state');
examples.explanation: A valid empty response should not be treated as an error.

examples.title: Handle status first
examples.code:
const status=503;
console.log(status<500?'inspect response':'service error path');
examples.explanation: Status handling can decide which response path to follow.

examples.title: Map data for display
examples.explanation: Display logic should handle missing fields safely.

commonMistakes: Starting implementation without defining scope or acceptance criteria.
Combining input, logic, and display in one tangled block.
Claiming features or data persist when they are only in memory.
Adding features before the core workflow works and is tested.

guidedTask.title: Guided Project
guidedTask.instructions: Build a small consumer for a mocked API response. Start with a fixed JSON fixture, validate status and shape, map data into a display-friendly list, and handle empty/error states. Keep live credentials out of the project.
steps: Build a small consumer for a mocked API response. Start with a fixed JSON fixture, validate status and shape, map data into a display-friendly list, and handle empty/error states. Keep live credentials out of the project.
Write a short scope and acceptance checklist.
Test a normal case and at least two edge/error cases.

independentTask.title: Independent Project
independentTask.instructions: Create a toy API consumer design or implementation using mocked data or a public API with appropriate safeguards. Include request configuration, parsing, validation, UI states, timeout, error handling, and tests.
requirements: Keep the project original and appropriately scoped.

Create a toy API consumer design or implementation using mocked data or a public API with appropriate safeguards. Include request configuration, parsing, validation, UI states, timeout, error handling, and tests.
Include a short test plan and results.

hints: Use mock fixtures before connecting to a real service.
Represent loading, success, empty, and error states.
Never put secret credentials in a public client.
